# The Millbrook Bridge Decision

## A Routine Inspection Turns Up Trouble

Every two years, an inspection team walks the Millbrook Bridge—a 62-year-old steel truss structure carrying State Route 9 over the Millbrook River. Like most bridges, it gets a routine visual inspection on a fixed schedule. Inspectors look for rust, cracks, loose bolts, concrete spalling (where chunks break off exposing rebar), and signs that the deck has settled or shifted. They tap areas with hammers, take measurements, and photograph anything suspicious. Each bridge component gets rated on a scale from "excellent" down to "imminent failure."

At the last routine inspection, the inspector noticed something that warranted a closer look: corrosion on two of the main girder connections, and a hairline crack near a weld on a floor beam—the beam that carries the road deck and transfers its weight to the main trusses. This triggered a "special inspection" with more sophisticated tools: ultrasonic testing to measure crack depth, instruments that listen for the acoustic signature of growing cracks, and load-rating calculations to determine how much weight the bridge can safely carry.
